meta.audience: The Nephites who would keep their liberty
meta.location: Zarahemla and the land round about
principles: One man's effect on a nation
A covenant made with torn clothing
A name taken gladly that was given in contempt

world_behind.title: The dissension of Alma 45 acquires a leader
world_behind.text: Verse 3 names Amalickiah, and verse 4 says he wanted to be king. The people who would not hear Helaman now have somebody to follow.

world_behind.title: His base is the lower judges
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says they were the greater part of them lower judges seeking power, and verse 5 gives his offer: support him and be made rulers. Mosiah 29:28 and 29 had built the lower judges as a check on the higher ones; forty years on, that same tier is the constituency a would-be king recruits from first.

world_behind.title: Mormon stops to state a rule
world_behind.text: Verses 8 through 10 say how quick men forget God, and how far the damage from a single wicked man reaches. He interrupts the narrative to say it.

world_behind.title: Moroni writes on a piece of his own coat
world_behind.text: Verse 12 gives the six words written on the rent coat and verse 13 names it the title of liberty. Alma 62:4 to 5 has him raise the same standard in a later crisis, and 3 Nephi 3:2 has an enemy commander praise the Nephites for keeping what they call their liberty. The phrase outlives the cloth.

world_behind.title: Christian is a name outsiders used
world_behind.text: Verses 14 and 15 explain that those outside the church called believers Christians, and that the believers took the name gladly. Acts 11 records the same at Antioch.

world_behind.title: The covenant is made with clothing
world_behind.text: Verses 21 and 22 have the people rend their garments and cast them at Moroni's feet as a token of their covenant. Mosiah 18:10 and Alma 24:17 record the two earlier mass covenants in the book, one made at a water and one over buried weapons; this is the third, and the only one made with clothing.

world_behind.title: The rent coat is read back to Joseph
world_behind.text: Verses 23 through 27 tie the torn coat to Joseph's coat and to a prophecy of Jacob about a remnant of it preserved. Genesis 37:31 to 33 carries the coat itself; the prophecy Moroni quotes about the preserved remnant is on the brass plates and appears nowhere in the Bible, which is why 1 Nephi 5:14 matters for reading this passage.

words.text: The Nephite dissenter who becomes king of the Lamanites. The name occurs sixty-four times in this record, all in Alma 46 through 51. Mormon introduces him as a large and strong man before saying anything about his aims.

Agreeable speech used to gain something. The plural occurs once in this record and three times in the King James Bible, all in Daniel 11, of a king who obtains a kingdom by them. Amalickiah's method is named before his first act.
Uncertain, dependent on something that may fail. The word occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it of Nephite affairs immediately after a great victory, which is the point he draws in verse 8.

Believers in Christ. The word occurs four times in this record and once in the King James Bible, where the disciples are first called Christians at Antioch. Mormon says it began as an outsider's label and was taken up gladly.
A sign that stands for something. The people rend their garments in token, and Mormon glosses it in the same clause as a covenant. The gesture and its meaning are supplied together.

What is left of something after most is gone. It appears sixty times in the record, and the King James Bible ninety-two. Moroni uses it four times in two verses, of Joseph's seed and of Joseph's coat, and makes the two the same argument.

phrases.term: They had been led by the flatteries of Amalickiah
phrases.text: Mormon gives the mechanism before the movement. The offer was rank in exchange for support, and the men who took it were already judges.

phrases.term: Thus we see how quick the children of men do forget the Lord their God
phrases.text: Mormon breaks off to say it. The victory of Alma 44 and the rejoicing of Alma 45 are three verses behind, and the dissension is already underway.

phrases.term: The great wickedness one very wicked man can cause
phrases.text: The chapter's second stated rule. Mormon has just described a movement and attributes it to a single person, and the next six chapters follow that person.

phrases.term: He rent his coat; and he took a piece thereof, and wrote upon it
phrases.text: The making of the standard, described as an act rather than a design. Moroni tears his own clothing, writes six things on it, and fastens it to a pole.

phrases.term: In memory of our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children
phrases.text: The full text of the title of liberty. Alma 43:45 had given nearly the same list as what the Nephites fought for, so the banner puts an existing argument into words.

phrases.term: So long as there should a band of Christians remain to possess the land
phrases.text: The term of Moroni's prayer. He asks for liberty on the land for as long as believers hold it, which makes the blessing conditional on who is there.

phrases.term: Took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ
phrases.text: A name coined by opponents and adopted by the people it was aimed at. Mormon supplies the origin in verse 14 and the reception in verse 15.

phrases.term: Until we bring it upon us by our own transgressions
phrases.text: Moroni states the one way the promise fails. He is claiming protection and naming its limit in the same sentence, as he did to Zerahemnah in Alma 44.

phrases.term: The Lord should rend them even as they had rent their garments
phrases.text: The covenant, given in the form of the gesture that seals it. The people ask for the treatment their clothing has just received if they break it.

phrases.term: Even as we have cast our garments at thy feet to be trodden under foot
phrases.text: The people's own words, extending the figure. They name the land northward as the precedent for what destruction looks like.

phrases.term: Even as this remnant of garment of my son hath been preserved
phrases.text: Jacob's prophecy, quoted by Moroni over a torn coat on a pole. The argument runs from a preserved piece of cloth to a preserved piece of a family.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: Built first, named second
verses.text: The record introduces the man by his position and his body before it gives his name: "the leader of those who were wroth against their brethren was a large and a strong man; and his name was Amalickiah." Size is the only physical fact the chapter supplies about anyone. The name then takes over: it stands fifteen times in these forty-one verses, which is second among the nine chapters of the volume that use it at all, behind Alma 47 with twenty-six.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: The writing on the cloth, given exactly
verses.text: The record does not paraphrase what was written on the torn coat. It reproduces it: "In memory of our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children." Six nouns, and the last two are the domestic ones. Verse 13 then names the object, "he called it the title of liberty," and verse 19 insists on the point of the writing, that he waved it "that all might see the writing which he had written." Three verses of the volume carry the phrase title of liberty: two here, and Alma 51:20.

verses.label: v. 20–22
verses.title: A covenant done with the hands
verses.text: The proclamation asks people to "enter into a covenant," and what follows is not an oath but an action: they come running "with their armor girded about their loins, rending their garments in token" and cast the pieces at Moroni's feet. Then their words are given too, beginning "We covenant with our God, that we shall be destroyed, even as our brethren in the land northward." The formula enter into a covenant holds the chapter together, standing at verse 20 where it is proposed, verse 31 where the army is described by it, and verse 35 where refusing it is fatal.

verses.label: v. 23–26
verses.title: A saying of Jacob that Genesis does not carry
verses.text: Moroni's argument rests on a quotation, and the record marks it as one at both ends. Verse 24 opens "let us remember the words of Jacob, before his death," gives the saying about a preserved part of Joseph's coat, and verse 26 closes it: "Now behold, this was the language of Jacob." The Bible mentions Joseph's coat in five verses, all in Genesis 37, and none of them concerns a surviving fragment; Jacob's dying words in Genesis 49 say nothing about it. The volume itself uses coat of Joseph and remnant of the coat in this one verse and nowhere else. Whatever its source, the chapter treats it as a text its hearers already know.

verses.label: v. 27
verses.title: The argument turned on the arguer
verses.text: Having applied the preserved fragment to his own side, Moroni asks who the perishing remainder might be, and gives two answers in one sentence: "who knoweth but what the remnant of the seed of Joseph, which shall perish as his garment, are those who have dissented from us? Yea, and even it shall be ourselves if we do not stand fast in the faith of Christ." The rhetorical question is set up to indict the dissenters and then finished so that it can land on the speaker. A banner argument that stopped one clause earlier would have been a straightforward war speech.

verses.label: v. 34–35
verses.title: Authority stated, then used
verses.text: Verse 34 is careful about where the power comes from: Moroni was "appointed by the chief judges and the voice of the people, therefore he had power according to his will with the armies." Verse 35 reports what he did with it: whoever "would not enter into a covenant to support the cause of freedom, that they might maintain a free government, he caused to be put to death." The record offers no comment on the sentence, no number of the executed, and no objection from anyone. The constitutional basis stands in verse 34, the killing in verse 35, and nothing follows either.

verses.label: v. 40–41
verses.title: A war chapter that ends on medicine
verses.text: After the banner, the covenant and the executions, the last two verses turn to how people died of natural causes. Some died of fevers, "but not so much so with fevers, because of the excellent qualities of the many plants and roots which God had prepared to remove the cause of diseases." Then the closing sentence marks itself as a guess: those who died in faith "are happy in him, as we must needs suppose." That phrase is used twice in the volume, here and at 2 Ne. 2:17, and both times a writer is flagging his own inference rather than reporting.

chapter.title: Mormon names the cause as one man
chapter.text: He interrupts to say how much damage one very wicked man can do, and then spends six chapters showing it. The generalization is stated before the evidence is given.

chapter.title: The banner is made out of what Moroni was wearing
chapter.text: No workshop, no design. He tears his coat, writes on it, and puts it on a stick, and the record treats the improvisation as the point.

chapter.title: Six words carry the cause
chapter.text: God, religion, freedom, peace, wives, children. Alma 43 had listed nearly the same as the reason for fighting, so the banner condenses an argument the reader has already had.

chapter.title: The protection is claimed with its limit attached
chapter.text: Verse 18 says God will not suffer them to be destroyed until they bring it on themselves. Moroni states the escape clause in the middle of the promise.

chapter.title: The covenant is enacted, not recited
chapter.text: Torn garments cast at a commander's feet, with the people supplying the terms. The physical act is the wording.

chapter.title: A slur is adopted as a name
chapter.text: Christians was what outsiders called them, and the believers took it gladly. Mormon records both halves and does not comment.

chapter.title: The argument reaches back to Genesis
chapter.text: Joseph's rent coat, a preserved remnant, Jacob's prophecy about the seed. Moroni ties a torn coat in his hand to a torn coat six hundred years back.

chapter.title: The chapter ends with plants
chapter.text: The last two verses turn from war to medicine and mortality. Verse 40 names the illness, the season, and the remedy, "some who died with fevers, which at some seasons of the year were very frequent in the land—but not so much so with fevers, because of the excellent qualities of the many plants and roots which God had prepared to remove the cause of diseases." Verse 41 then records the ordinary deaths, "many who died with old age," and closes on a hedge, "as we must needs suppose." A chapter of banners and oaths ends on epidemiology and an admission of uncertainty.

applications.title: Price the promotion that comes with the praise
applications.text: Amalickiah's supporters were lower judges who had been told they would be made rulers over the people. When someone's flattery arrives attached to an advancement they are offering you, work out what the advancement is worth to them before you weigh the flattery.

applications.title: Watch what follows a victory
applications.text: Nephite affairs turned precarious right after a deliverance. When something has gone well, that is the moment to check what is slipping.

applications.title: Write down what you are for
applications.text: Moroni put six words on a piece of cloth. Name the handful of things you would actually defend, in words short enough to remember under pressure.

applications.title: Take the name they meant as an insult
applications.text: Believers were called Christians by people outside and took it gladly. When a label aimed at you is accurate, owning it takes the sting out.

applications.title: Make the ask visible and exact
applications.text: Moroni waved the writing so everyone could see it and then named the precise commitment he wanted made. A general appeal for support collects nodding; a stated covenant with the words in view collects people running.

applications.title: Make the commitment physical
applications.text: The people rent their garments and cast them down. When you decide something important, do something concrete that you will remember doing.

applications.title: Ask whether the warning fits you
applications.text: Moroni read Jacob's prophecy onto the dissenters and then said "even it shall be ourselves" if his own people did not stand fast. When you hold up a cautionary example about somebody else, finish the thought by testing whether the same reading fits your side of it.

applications.title: Put the standard where it stays in view
applications.text: The title of liberty went up on every tower in the land instead of being shown once at the gathering. A commitment announced at a meeting fades; one you walk past every morning is harder to forget.

questions.text: What would someone have to offer me to buy my support?
How quickly do I forget what I was grateful for last month?
If I had one piece of cloth, what six words would I write?
What am I willing to pray for out loud, in front of people?
What is the one thing that could bring trouble on me, by my own doing?
What have I promised without doing anything to mark it?
What remnant am I part of?

targets.markdown: And **when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch**. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.

entries.head: Dan. 11:21

anchor.quote: led by the flatteries of Amalickiah

entries.reason: a king obtaining a kingdom by the same means

targets.quote: obtain the kingdom by flatteries.
targets.verse_text: And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.
targets.markdown: And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and **obtain the kingdom by flatteries**.

markers.quote: And Amalickiah was desirous to be a king;
led by the flatteries of Amalickiah,
the great wickedness one very wicked man can cause to take place
he led away the hearts of many people to do wickedly;
In memory of our God, our religion, and freedom
he called it the title of liberty)
took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ,
or Christians as they were called
until we bring it upon us by our own transgressions
be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ,
even as we have cast our garments at thy feet to be trodden under foot,
whose coat was rent by his brethren into many pieces
let us remember the words of Jacob, before his death,
a remnant of the seed of my son be preserved
Amalickiah fled with a small number of his men,
thus Moroni planted the standard of liberty among the Nephites.
